text: Calculus II with Dr. Miller was a mixed bag for me. I came in with a genuine curiosity about the topic, but the vibe you get from the lectures is that the explanations drift and the room for interpretation in the instructions feels a bit too wide, which didn’t help my mostly-recordings-and-notes attendance pattern. I have a strong coding background but weak theory, so the jump from intuition to formal proofs left me flipping through forums and office hours more than I’d like. The feedback timing was frustrating: the grading comments were detailed, yet they showed up long after I’d already needed to move on to the next assignment, which made it hard to adjust my approach quickly. The assessments felt like they didn’t map neatly to what was being lectured, and the deadlines stacked up in a way that felt unplanned, not just heavy. The LMS and submission flow were smooth, which saved me a lot of friction on busy weeks, and I did dial into a few TA office hours when a project-style problem appeared. Still, I wouldn’t take it again, even though it did push some useful ideas into my toolkit.

I took Operating Systems this summer mainly to fit the schedule, and I’ll admit the pace felt brutal alongside two other demanding courses and a full-time job. The project-heavy load and a few high-stakes exams wore me down, especially with the mid-semester crunch and the grading that came with long, detailed comments but took forever to show up. The rubric felt vague at times, and while the prerequisites built nicely, I’d only recommend it if you’re prepared to plan around slow feedback and patchy deadlines.

I kept up with almost every lecture in Cyber Security Basics, but the workload felt heavier than I expected for first semester, especially trying to fit short evening sessions around everything. The tool setup was frustrating, and deadlines during the weeks those issues hit felt impossible to manage, even though feedback did come quickly enough to adjust. I don’t think I’d take it again, though it did help in spots. I remember asking Prof. Rios a late-night question in the forum about a weird error on the lab, and he replied before sunrise.

I took Database Systems in the summer term because I heard it would be useful for industry work, and Prof. Haddad kept things moving despite the compressed pace. I used the materials selectively, and the quick feedback helped me adjust on the fly, though some comments arrived too late to salvage a couple late assignments; the mix of fair but exhausting assessments kept me on my toes. The work felt mostly solo, with a few practicals like the small schema project I did using a local MySQL instance, and I’m genuinely enthusiastic about the practical edge it gave me, even if I’m not sure I’d do it again under the same sprinty timeline.

I took Database Systems mainly because I needed it for a specialization and I’m juggling a full-time job, so I fell behind for a stretch and managed to catch up around a few deadlines. Dr. Chen is solid—clear lectures, practical explanations, and the LMS submission flow actually felt smooth, which helped when I only had evenings to work. The grading rubric felt vague, and the assessment mix didn’t quite line up with what the lectures covered, which was frustrating during the midterm project. Mostly I did solo work, and while the course stayed useful, I didn’t really enjoy it the way I hoped; it just felt like a necessary skill rather than something engaging. Still, I’d recommend it to others with similar time constraints.

Calculus II with Dr. Miller started strong in intuition, but the examples stayed thin and the grading rubric felt vague. I fell behind around midterms, then caught up only by sprinting to deadlines; motivation stayed genuine, though collaboration felt unclear.

Midway through a heavy semester, I’m still sorting through the Machine Learning stuff Dr. Park tosses at us. The materials are solid and I appreciated a few clear proofs, though the software stack starts rough and only gradually becomes manageable. It helps to study in a group; alone I’d have struggled more with the tooling setup and the forum replies can feel a bit dismissive, but I managed the deadlines while juggling a full-time job. Overall, I’m not sure I’d recommend without caveats.

Midway through a heavy semester, I’m new to the field and just trying to keep up; slides are serviceable but not memorable, and tooling glitches during deadlines made week crunches feel worse. Still, group work clicked if the team ran smoothly.

Thinking back, Data Structures felt like I walked in rusty and came out with a few rusty screws still loose, especially once mid-semester crunch hit and my attendance faded from the initial spark of curiosity to a tired, “just get it done” mode. Prof. Haddad seemed sharp, but the course moved so fast that I kept second-guessing whether I was following the thread or just reacting to deadlines stacked every week; the assignment-heavy pace didn’t help my rhythm as a returning student trying to reorient. The email support felt slow during those tight weeks, which left me stuck on a couple of algorithms projects that mattered for the next due date, and the lack of quick guidance only amplified that sense of scrambling. The structure was mostly solo work, with few chances to bounce ideas off peers, and I kept thinking about an early confusion I had about asymptotic analyses that colored the rest of the term and made everything feel heavier than it needed to be. A small thing I won’t forget is the one project where I had to implement a custom hash table under a tight deadline; it felt doable in isolation but the clock forced a shaky finish, and that lingering fatigue is what still sticks with me.

I’d say my take on Computer Networks isn’t cleanly positive, even though I stuck with it as my main focus that term. Prof. Rios is fair enough in lectures, and the quick feedback to push me to adjust helped a bit, but the vibe was pretty dry and I felt like I was wading through packets more than learning concepts I could reuse. I leaned on the TAs—they were responsive and practical and kept me from sinking, especially during the week we juggled two hard classes. The LMS flow was smooth, and I liked that office hours finally lined up with my own schedule, though I still barely scraped by a barely-passed grade after a constant battle with the late-week labs and a stubborn grading quirk on the project.

I’m a returning student who felt rusty, and the summer term made the pace feel like a sprint with short rest breaks. The lectures were clear enough when we were in them, and the lecturer clearly knows their stuff, but the way the material is chunked into quick hits left me chasing the thread between sessions. The course builds on what’s stated in the prerequisites, which helped when I finally sat down and reconnected with SQL tuning concepts, yet I still wrestled with staying motivated on weeks when I didn’t have a big deadline looming. Tooling problems routinely derailed parts of the workflow, and deadlines piled up in a way that made weeks feel longer and more stressful than they needed to be. Feedback often showed up only after I’d moved past the relevant stage, which left me guessing whether I should revise or move on, and the assignments are heavy on tasks and light on steady, early guidance. A small cue I’ll remember: the team project required a specific schema tweak that wasn’t obvious until the last moment, which felt like a misstep in pacing more than a learning moment. Overall, I did gain solid concepts, but the cadence was rough and sometimes inconsistent.

I took Linear Algebra mostly because it fit my schedule more than I cared about the subject, and that made the early weeks feel optional yet the workload soon piled up. I fell behind and then caught up right around the deadlines, which meant a lot of frantic late-night reviews and a few quick, unclear feedback emails that came too late to actually help my next steps. Prof. Alvarez is reasonable in office hours, I remember one chat where we pinned the matrix sketch to a whiteboard and he explained a hack that helped me see why it mattered, but the platform quirks and the unclear collaboration expectations kept stirring up avoidable stress. It’s useful, not exactly enjoyable.

Dr. Chen is clearly good at teaching, and the lectures helped me grasp ideas, but attendance faded mid‑semester as workload spiked; the project-heavy setup and high-stakes exams stressed me more than the adjacent material I wish I’d known earlier.

I came into Machine Learning partly because I’d heard it would actually help in industry, and I’ll say Prof. Haddad knows his stuff, even if the week-to-week rhythm can feel uneven. I kept up with nearly every lecture because the topics clicked when he explained them, but the way feedback lands is frustratingly sparse until it’s almost too late to fix anything, which made the late deadlines and the assessment style feel exhausting rather than clarifying. The course design rewards you for connecting adjacent material you already know, which works if you’re comfortable with the surrounding math and algorithms, but it means you’ll struggle if you’re behind on a prereq thread. Tooling setup for the assignment environment was a pain, a real administrative frictions nightmare, and it made the first project feel heavier than it should have been. The assessments themselves were fair, yes, but they wore me out anyway, like there’s a steady drumbeat of fine print and edge cases to chase. I did notice that the instruction sometimes lands with more punch one week than the next, and I ended up shaping my study around short evening sessions rather than a consistent block, which felt like a workable compromise but didn’t fix the uneven delivery. Overall, I’d still say it was useful, if you’re prepared to slog through the setup, the pacing, and the late-stage feedback.

Data Structures was a useful intro for industry work, and the workload felt doable even as I fell behind and caught up around deadlines; lectures with Dr. Park were serviceable, slides fine but not memorable, LMS smooth, but grading comments came late sometimes.

Dr. Chen’s Machine Learning course was solid in how the lectures and slides mapped onto the prereqs, and I appreciated the clear examples, even if the grading rubric felt vague at times; I mainly relied on recordings and notes, and office hours once clarified a doubt about overfitting.

man, taking Database Systems in the middle of a brutal semester was rough, but the lectures felt solid and the lecturer explained things clearly when I caught them live, even if I mostly skimmed the slides and relied on recordings. the exam felt fair and my notes from the week felt like they lined up with the questions, though the workload was heavy with the big report and the fast feedback that came with it.

Linear Algebra was my first semester in the program, and I mostly lived off the recordings and notes once I realized the live lectures didn’t fit my week. The LMS flow; submitting homework and reusing the same rubric across topics kept things smooth, which helped since I kept this as my main focus course that term. The grade felt solid B and matched the effort I put in, though the feedback arrived a bit late to actually guide me on the last couple of assignments. I remember a turning point near the end when a late problem set clarified what I’d misunderstood about eigenvectors, but the timing meant I wasn’t able to adjust in time for the final push. Collaboration felt unclear—there were expectations about group work, but the boundaries and roles never gelled well for us, so I mostly worked solo and crossed fingers on the odd discussion post. Time pressure was manageable most weeks, and I appreciated that the platform didn’t pile on extra friction, but the sparse feedback until late hit hard when I was trying to recover from a midterm wobble. Mentally, I kept circling back to that late-semester moment; it anchored how I assessed the course after the dust settled.

I’m in the middle of a heavy semester and took Data Structures mostly out of curiosity, and I do feel like I learned some solid basics, especially around how different data representations actually influence performance. Prof. Alvarez presents slides that are serviceable but not memorable, and I often found myself wanting a bit more real-world context beyond the diagrams we chant through in class. The quick feedback cadence helps me adjust before things derail, which I appreciate, but the tooling setup to get started on assignments was frustrating enough to slow me down the first week. I fell behind and caught up around deadlines, which made the grading feel a touch inconsistent—like one week I’d get feedback already, the next it would show up late and make me second-guess my approach. The collaboration expectations feel unclear, so I mostly worked solo, though the course clearly expects teamwork on a project later. One memorable week was the midterm sprint where we had to implement a performance-focused trie under tight time pressure, which stuck with me more than the rest. Overall, I’m glad I took it, even if the grading logic didn’t always sit right with me.

I took Data Structures mainly because it fit my schedule more than I was excited about the topic, and I’m glad I did enough to check off the required course for my track. I’m comfortable with proofs, but I’m not big on systems work, so the explanations were mostly conceptual, with examples feeling a bit thin. The forums were sometimes helpful, but occasionally they felt dismissive when I asked about a shaky point in a proof, which didn’t help when deadlines stacked up in week seven. The peer discussions saved me more than the official materials, and the course builds reasonably well on the prerequisites, though I relied heavily on recordings and notes to keep up. A small note: there was this one project with a tricky swap-tree insert that stood out in my memory more than the lectures, and that’s honestly the anchor detail I’ll carry forward. The whole experience was a mix, learned a lot but kind of disliked the ride.

Taking Machine Learning while juggling a full-time job was… eye-opening in the wrong ways. Dr. Singh is clearly capable, but the way the course was run felt like it assumed I already knew more than I did and had all day to grind through dense readings. I relied mostly on recorded lectures and notes, and by week six I could feel the fatigue shaping my memory of the material rather than the ideas themselves, especially when the exam format changed last minute and the questions seemed to hinge on tiny details I hadn’t clocked from the recordings. The assessments were heavy on reports and deadlines stacked back-to-back, which ate into real study time and made it feel less about understanding concepts and more about churning pages of analysis before the clock ran out. Office hours helped a ton, but it still felt like a lifeboat rather than a steady guide through the storm. A single bright spot was a hands-on week where I finally connected a practical idea to something I’d read, even if it didn’t save the overall vibe. I’m not sure I’d recommend it in good conscience, given how overwhelming the prerequisites and exam pressure felt, but it’s not all useless either. The memory of that one Friday quiz week lingers because I relaxed for a minute and realized I’d misunderstood a core assumption.

Data Structures was a solid fit timing-wise for my last semester, and it did build nicely on prereqs, but the deadlines stacked up and the tooling hiccups made weeks feel rough; the recorded lectures were helpful yet dry, and I’d probably not take it again even though it nudged me past a tricky project.

This first semester in the program has been a sprint I'm juggling with a full-time job, so I appreciated Dr. Chen’s clearly explained lectures and steady pacing, even if I sometimes felt a beat behind with the platform quirks that add avoidable stress. The course is heavy on reports, and between that and multiple demanding courses, the feedback often lands too late to adjust my approach, which is frustrating. I’ve learned a lot, but I can’t shake the sense that the experience dragged a bit; it’s easier than the prerequisite, yet still feels like more time than I can really spare. I’d only recommend it if you’re prepared to grind through the weeks and tolerate some hiccups in timing and tools.

I took Data Structures mainly to fit my schedule, and Prof. Alvarez is solid, with organized lectures, though the prerequisite felt broader than advertised; group study helps a lot, and one memorable assignment week stuck during exam prep, but feedback varied.

I’m in the first semester of the program and took Linear Algebra with Prof. Haddad, and I’ll admit I came in with a strong coding background but pretty weak theory, so the ramp-up felt sharp. The workload nudged me to stay on top of it, and while the design of assessments was neutral to me, the tooling hiccups during deadline weeks made things feel extra stressful, as if the clock loomed larger than it should. The course leans toward mostly individual work, and I could tell the instruction delivery was uneven week to week, which didn’t help a lot when a key concept suddenly clicked only after I wandered back to the notes. One memorable week was the exam that felt part memorization, part quick reasoning—definitely a turning point, and I won’t forget it. I’d probably not take it again, but it did push me to fill gaps in theory I hadn’t cared about before.

The Machine Learning course felt like a rough ride mid‑semester, with lectures that varied week to week and a rubric that never quite spelled out what counted for a good grade. I started out engaged, but attendance faded as the evenings piled up, and the help from staff seemed sparse, so classmates became my main support. I learned a lot, but I genuinely disliked the experience overall and the grading felt vague. The sharp ramp after the approachable intro didn’t help.

Second-semester senior year, with too many deadlines in the same stretch, I stuck with Computer Networks more out of obligation than enthusiasm, and I can’t shake a weird mix of learning a ton and disliking the vibe. Prof. Alvarez gave quick feedback on the weekly labs and the big project, and the scores showed up fast, but the explanations felt skimpy—like I could see what I did wrong but not why, especially when the network-simulation results didn’t align with the packet-trace expectations. The tooling setup was a headache from week one, so the first few canvases of the project were spent wrestling with VPN access and the lab image, which eaten into the time I already didn’t have during that mid-semester crunch. The forums helped sometimes, but a few replies sounded dismissive, which didn’t help when I was stuck on the 802.11csomethings or trying to parse the exam-style questions that spun into high-stakes moments. I did end up learning a lot in the sense that I could critique throughput vs latency in a real-world subnetwork, yet I left the room feeling the whole thing wasn’t quite the right fit for how I learn, especially as I approach graduation. The one memory that sticks is the project kickoff with a muddy deadline pattern and a strange enthusiasm for a topic that never quite clicked into place.

Computer Networks felt like a rough start that I stuck with mostly because my schedule had room for it, not because I was excited by the topic. The exams were fair enough, but the whole setup—report-heavy work and a vague grading rubric—made the time pressure feel messy, especially since I was balancing another hard class; relying on recordings helped, but the first weeks with the software stack were a slog. One memorable week was the big assignment where the deadline loomed and I realized I hadn’t understood the tool at all until I blocked a full afternoon to grunge through it.

I stuck with Computer Networks as an advanced elective, trying to fit short evening sessions around my busy week, and the lectures were clear with decent pacing, which helped a bit when the material got dense. I liked the instructor a lot, they explained concepts well, but I left the grading feeling unsure about whether I actually understood the core ideas—the week of the big assignment and the exam didn’t align for me, and the feedback came too late to fix things. Tooling problems during deadline weeks made everything harder, and I found myself using the provided materials only when I needed a nudge to get through. Office hours saved the course a few times, though, and I’ll remember that one week where we had a tricky router-setup question as a kind of turning point.

Linear Algebra was my main focus this term, and the lectures moved at a clear pace, even as tool glitches and deadline week chaos dragged things out. I’m not sure the grade reflected my grasp, but the turning point happened when I finally saw the matrices click during a late-night practice set.

Dr. Park is solid, but the course felt uneven and left me curious more about the theory than the code. The recorded lectures helped, yet they’re dry; attendance faded mid‑semester, and the mix of assessments didn’t align with what was actually covered, especially near the big project. I remember asking about a tricky subnet topic in office hours and getting a detailed, helpful pointer after a week.

i’d say the course was halfway okay, but the slides were just serviceable and didn’t stick. office hours saved it for me, especially when i was juggling proofs and a tough systems project late at night. the tooling setup was a headache, though.

I kicked off Cyber Security Basics with decent momentum, and Prof. Haddad explained the concepts clearly enough, though I started to drift as attendance faded mid-semester once the schedule got busy. I made it the main focus that term, but the instructions often left room for interpretation, which was frustrating during the midterm prep. TAs were responsive and practical, and peer discussions helped more than the official materials, especially when we debated the safer configurations for that lab project.

Overall, I came away feeling the course was surprisingly useful for how little I enjoyed the process sometimes. I’m glad I stuck with it because the networking concepts clicked when I could connect them to my coding background, even if the motivation wavered mid-semester. The project-heavy setup and some high-stakes exams meant I had to chunk time oddly and use the materials only when it helped me finish a concrete task, like debugging a packet-flow model I built for a late-night sprint. Tool setup felt like a barrier more than a bridge, and I wish the prerequisite material had clicked earlier, since adjacent topics would have helped me coast through the tougher days. Still, when the team worked, we actually got somewhere, which kept me going.

So I’m a returning student who feels rusty, and Data Structures was the middle-of-a-heavy-semester grind I saw coming. The lectures were clear with decent pacing, but the exam felt unfair—like a few questions veered into edge cases that didn’t line up with the week’s focus, and I left wondering if the grading favored recall over real understanding. The software stack started rough for me at first, then settled into something manageable, though the tool quirks still nipped at me during the midterm crunch. I compared it to another course from this term and it’s fair to say this one demands you already know the adjacent material, which didn’t help my timing, but the fast score feedback helped me adjust quickly, even if explanations were thin. Overall, it’s a solid challenge, just not as fair as I hoped.

The course felt like a solid challenge for my first semester, with exams that aren’t a cakewalk but fair enough to study toward. The quick feedback helped adjust, though the workload was heavy and the week-to-week pace can feel uneven, especially around the big report deadline.

I’m a returning student and felt rusty in mid‑semester chaos, but Prof. Haddad still lands solidly on the core OS ideas, even if the weeks feel uneven and the tooling hiccups make deadline weeks rough. The forums help sometimes, but a few replies read dismissive, and grading comments arrive late yet are pretty detailed when they do show up—like the project feedback pinpoints a real misstep I made on page tables, which I still remember.

I came into Machine Learning in my last semester hoping it’d be a bridge to industry, but the exam felt unfair and left me clutching at straws during the last two weeks of revision. I started off engaged, but my attendance faded mid‑semester as the lectures started to drag, even though the recorded videos were convenient. Prof. Haddad is clearly knowledgeable, and the LMS submission flow is smooth, but the assessment mix didn’t match what we actually learned in class, which was frustrating. A memorable week was the big, timed quiz right after a long weekend—felt like a trap, not a fair test of what we covered. Still, it wasn’t all bad: the tooling vibe was fine, and I did pick up a few practical ideas I’ll keep.

Linear Algebra felt a bit rusty coming back, and I mostly relied on the recording lectures and notes instead of a steady attendance pattern. The slides are serviceable but not memorable, and the way the instructions leave a lot open to interpretation made the prerequisites feel bigger than advertised; I spent more time decoding what was expected than actually solving problems. There were only a few assessments, but each one carried a ton of weight, so one awkward week in the middle of the term felt like it could tank the curve for everyone. Compared to the easier prerequisite, this course demanded more prior intuition than I expected, and I’m not sure I’d recommend it when you’re juggling multiple demanding classes, though I did find one memorable week of a tough, clocked quiz that stuck with me.

I came into Linear Algebra expecting to handle proofs and left realizing the lectures were a bit dry, though the lecturer explained concepts clearly enough to fill in gaps I had from not doing much systems-work before. The forum and TA hours helped, especially when I could bounce questions about eigenvectors after a late-night problem set, but the collaboration stuff felt murky and attendance faded mid‑semester. There was a turning point near the end when I finally got how the abstract ideas clicked, but the delayed, detailed grading comments kept catching me off guard.

Overall, the course felt well organized and useful for real-world work, especially since I could fit short evening sessions around my schedule in the last semester. I started engaged, but attendance faded mid-semester as deadlines piled up, and the quick feedback helped me adjust, though the email support tends to drag when we're chasing a due date. One concrete pain point: the collaboration expectations felt unclear, which made the team project feel messy even though the lectures had solid structure.

Midway through this heavy term, I’ll say the course has its usefulness, even if it isn’t the most enjoyable ride. Dr. Park lectures can be solid and clear, especially when a topic clicks, but the delivery feels uneven week to week, like some sessions land and others drift. The project-heavy setup and the high-stakes exams push you to hustle, yet I appreciated how quickly feedback arrives enough to adjust, which helped me keep some momentum despite inconsistent motivation. The forums can be helpful but sometimes feel dismissive, and I still rely on them. I won’t pretend I’d recommend it to everyone, but there are real bits that land if you’re stubborn about grinding through it.

I took Computer Networks last semester out of genuine curiosity, and while the lectures felt dry, the workload was manageable with steady behind-then-full-til-deadlines effort; exam fairness surprised me, and I barely expected to learn so much despite platform quirks and heavy assignments.

I’m a returning student who felt rusty, and Calculus II started accessible but ramps up fast; the lectures were clear and well-paced, but the deadlines soured my motivation as the assignment load piled up. The TAs were practical and responsive, yet I still left the late-semester turning point frustrated, unsure I’d keep up.

I’m in my last semester and took Data Structures mostly because it fit my schedule more than because I felt drawn to the material, which didn’t help my motivation. I used the lecture slides and code examples only when I needed them, since I’m new to the discipline and still learning the basics, and I found the pacing a bit rough for someone starting from scratch. The LMS flow is fine and submissions are smooth, but feedback quality varies a lot by assignment, which left me unsure what to fix for the next one. I won’t take it again, even though it did help me get a foothold, and compared to the other course I took this term, the exam week memory still stings more than any project.

I took Operating Systems last semester while working full-time, and I’ll admit I started off engaged but attendance faded as deadlines piled up. The course filled some gaps for me, and the peer discussions saved a lot of the week—the official materials felt dry next to what my lab group talked through. The grading was a grind, with a heavy report focus and a few late email replies when I missed a deadline, but I genuinely enjoyed the vibe of the class more than the lecturer’s pace.

First-semester, required OS course left me unsure whether my C reflected real understanding; setup chores were tedious, slides serviceable but forgettable. Grading felt fair yet exhausting, with fast-but-thin feedback. I’d recommend only with solid prep and a memory of that midterm crunch.

First semester in this program and I kept up with nearly every lecture, but that grading rubric feels vague and makes it hard to know what’s really aimed for. Prof. Alvarez explains concepts clearly, though the fast ramp from accessible to tough hit my mid-semester crunch hard, and the few assessments felt high-stakes even though there aren’t many of them. Still, quick feedback helps when I’m scrambling to finish a late-night prototype for the data structure project.

Starting engaged, I started missing some classes mid-semester and the lectures felt dry, but the project on process scheduling was concrete and helped me grasp the ideas, even if the grading felt like it didn’t reflect my understanding. Overall, I’d recommend with solid prep.

I did fine overall, though I was often just barely keeping up. Dr. Miller is solid, exams felt fair, and the notes helped, but tooling glitches stretched deadlines and the explanations were sometimes thin—still, study groups and forums kept me advancing.

I’d say my takeaways were solid, but the experience felt uneven week to week. Park’s lectures are clear when they land, yet tooling delays and group churn during a big project week dragged things down more than I expected.

The OS course started rough for me as a returning student, and the exam felt unfairly stingy for a summer, compressed pacing where I kept tripping on tricky edge-case questions. Yet the recorded lectures helped me get back into the rhythm, and the TAs were practical and quick to respond when I asked about process scheduling quirks. I’m glad it builds on the prereqs, but I’m not sure I’d take it again.

This course felt tougher than I expected for an advanced elective, and I barely scraped by after burning out around deadlines. Dr. Park was fair about the exams, but the project-heavy setup and the vague instructions left me guessing at every turn; I often felt behind, then somehow caught up right near the cutoff. The software stack started rough but became manageable, and I’d say the turning point came when I finally stopped overthinking the prerequisites and just brute-forced the core data modeling tasks.

I took Calculus II in the summer so the pacing was brutal and I was juggling a full‑time job, which made the schedule feel like a tight fit rather than a passion project. The software stack started rough but settled into something usable, and I kept leaning on peers for quick problem fixes because staff weren’t as responsive as I hoped. A concrete moment: I looped back to the same forum thread the night before our midterm to verify a graphing trick, and that tiny win helped more than the lecture, even though the overall assessment mix never quite lined up with the lecture style.

I’m glad I stuck with Linear Algebra, but it felt like I barely scraped through and I’m still not sure what the grading was based on. Prof. Cohen’s lectures are okay, slides serve as a rough map but they aren’t memorable, and I had to fit study around short evening sessions, which meant I fell behind and then scrambled to catch up around deadlines. The mix of assessments didn’t line up with what we covered in class, and it felt like more prior math vibes were assumed than advertised, so I spent extra time relearning basics on my own. Group work can be useful when the team actually coordinates, otherwise it adds stress. A few moments stood out—like the late-night project tweaks and the little tool hiccup on the submission portal—but overall I learned a lot while disliking parts of the ride.

Taking OS with Prof. Alvarez in my last semester before graduation, I appreciated the clear lectures and decent pacing, especially since I’m coming from a strong coding background but weak on the theory side. The office hours felt like rescue sessions when I got stuck on the report-heavy twists of the project and deadlines started piling up, and that helped more than the slides did. Most work was solo, which was fine for time pressure most weeks, though I wish there was a bit more peer discussion to break up the solo grind. Overall it felt useful for the specialization, even if I didn’t enjoy it at every turn.

Taking Database Systems in my first semester, I had enough time but motivation was inconsistent, and I barely scraped a passing grade after a rough stretch midterm. Dr. Chen explains concepts clearly, and the materials are solid—well-structured slides and readable readings that helped when I revisited topics after long gaps. The organization is decent and feedback comes quickly enough to adjust, though the grading rubric felt vague at first, which didn’t help my early confusion that echoed throughout the term. Mostly individual work with little peer dependency; I wish the prerequisite fit were stronger for someone like me who didn’t fully chase adjacent material. One late-night bug in the project stood out as a memory anchor, shaping how I attacked the rest of the term.

Dr. Chen is a solid lecturer, and I found parts of Calculus II really click when he explains the core ideas, even if the week-to-week delivery felt a bit uneven. I relied on the materials only when I needed them, and the grading surprised me: I earned a solid B that lined up with the effort I actually put in, though the feedback quality varied a lot by assignment. The course works better with a study group, and the tooling setup was frustrating enough to slow me down at times. I admits mixed feelings here.

Taking Cyber Security Basics in my last semester before graduation, I appreciated the strong conceptual explanations, but the examples felt thin and the collaboration expectations were unclear; tooling setup was frustrating, and I’m still unsure if my C reflects true understanding, though I’d recommend it only with preparation. In office hours after a messy queue, I remember a concrete chat about threat models that actually helped.

Calculus II with Dr. Chen ended up being the main focus of my term, since I needed it for a specialization, and I’m glad I stuck with it even though the lectures often felt dry when I watched the recorded sessions later. The materials were solid and helpful, and the TAs were practical and responsive when I pinged them with quick questions, which saved me more than once. I did notice the platform quirks—some quirks caused avoidable stress around deadlines—so I had to stay on top of the interface more than I hoped. By the late-semester turning point, when we finally tied the networking model to the real-world outages I’d seen at work, it clicked enough to feel earned, even if I resent the tech hiccups that kept gnawing at momentum. Overall it fit the track and prerequisites, but the experience was more about surviving the deadlines than mastering the material in a relaxed way.

Feedback came quickly for graded items, but the explanations behind the scores felt thin, like I was told what was wrong without enough guidance on how to fix it, which was frustrating given the time pressure was manageable most weeks. The collaboration expectations felt unclear, and I wasn’t sure who was coordinating what, which made the team parts feel a bit stumbled. Compared to another course from the same term, this one was more demanding in the hands-on bits, and I remember a late-semester hiccup with a tool API that set back our progress for a day, but that didn’t derail everything. Overall, I’d call it useful but a bit user-unfriendly in setup.

Calculus II with Dr. Park was a mixed bag I’m still chewing on. I went in out of genuine curiosity, but the summer term pace felt brutal; the tooling glitches during deadlines didn’t help, and the mismatch between what we were told to study and what showed up in tests was annoying. Office hours rescued the course, and peer discussions somehow carried more weight than the official materials. Would not take it again, but it did push me to push through.

Taking Operating Systems during my first semester back in the program felt like trying to reassemble a puzzle I’d dumped out years ago, and I’m still surprised I managed to pass while juggling a full-time job. Prof. Rios is clearly knowledgeable, but the instructions left a lot of room for interpretation, which meant I spent more time guessing what counts as a “complete” submission than actually coding the OS concepts. The course felt very assignment-heavy with deadlines chugging along—three major pulls a week, plus smaller checks—and the fast scoring, with explanations that were thin, didn’t help me recover fast when I slipped. I relied on office hours a few times, and there was one session where we hashed out a locking issue in the project together; that moment stuck because the TA eased me past the vague rubric and pointed me to a clearer path, which I wish had happened sooner. I compared this term to another class I took simultaneously that felt calmer despite similar workload, and I kept thinking if OS could be more prescriptive rather than letting us infer the expected rigor. Email support was slow as deadlines loomed, which added tangible stress, but the core ideas in the lectures did land, even if the timing didn’t.

The lectures were recorded, which helped since I started my last semester juggling a full-time job, but the material felt dry and fast at times. I’m new to networks, so the early modules that are accessible slowly ramp up, and by midterm I was scrambling to keep up with the pace. I barely passed after a term of wrestling with the project deadline patterns and an anxious scramble for notes; I’d only recommend it if you’re ready to prep in advance and perhaps form a study group.

The Database Systems course was solid overall, with clear lectures and decent pacing, but the grading felt oddly generous after the curve and the instructions left too much room for interpretation. I managed time well amid other tough courses, but attendance faded mid-semester, and I’d only recommend it if you come in prepared.

Calculus II was a necessary grind for my specialization, and I barely scraped by after juggling it with a full-time job. The exams felt unfairly punishing, and the materials were a slog to pull together week by week, though the lectures moved at a decent pace. I remember a late-semester turning point when a tricky integration problem finally clicked after a rushed practice set, but the overall collaboration expectations remained murky and the report-heavy workload kept dragging on.

Took Cyber Security Basics mid‑semester while juggling a full-time job; felt rusty at first but the project-heavy setup kept me moving. The platform quirks and late feedback didn’t help, and I think the prerequisites assumed more background than advertised, though some parts clicked.

The Data Structures course felt doable at first, but mid-semester the workload spiked and the project-heavy setup with high-stakes exams exhausted me; I started attending less, despite group study help from classmates, and the tooling setup kept tripping me up before the big midterm.
